paragraphs: Estimating a changing hidden state from discrete events, such as neural spikes, is generally computationally intractable when done optimally. Numerical sampling can produce useful estimates, but it can be harder to see from those computations why a particular encoding or decoding strategy works. This paper develops a Bayesian approximation designed to make that reasoning analytically manageable.

The framework allows the researchers to describe sensory cell properties through distributions. This makes it easier to investigate neural populations that depart from uniform coding assumptions. Instead of treating numerical performance as the only outcome, the approach supports analysis of how the distribution of cell properties relates to the information available for estimating a state.

The resulting analysis produces insights that are difficult to obtain from numerical algorithms and is consistent with experiments concerning the locations of tuning curve centers. One finding is that silence can matter: the absence of spikes may provide information crucial to performance. This is a qualified finding about the value of non-events, supported by an approximate filtering framework.
neurips-2015-a-tractable-approximation-t.tldr: An analytically tractable Bayesian filtering approximation helps explain neural encoding and shows that the absence of spikes may be crucial information.

paragraphs: This paper adapts attention-based recurrent sequence generation to speech recognition. Attention lets a model condition its next output on selected parts of an input sequence. A direct adaptation of a machine translation model achieves a competitive 18.6% phoneme error rate on TIMIT, but it works only for utterances roughly as long as those used during training.

The researchers examine this failure qualitatively and introduce a generic way to make attention aware of location. The change gives the attention mechanism information about positions in the input, addressing the difficulty encountered when processing longer sequences. The resulting model achieves 18% phoneme error on single utterances and 20% on repeated utterances that are ten times longer.

A further modification prevents attention from concentrating excessively on individual frames and reduces phoneme error to 17.6%. The results identify two useful aspects of attention design for speech: handling input location and controlling concentration. The long-input evidence specifically comes from repeated utterances, while the reported error reductions establish the effectiveness of the proposed modifications in the evaluated task.
neurips-2015-attention-based-models-for-.tldr: Adding location awareness and limiting excessive concentration makes speech-recognition attention more robust to long inputs and reduces phoneme errors.

paragraphs: This paper develops an algorithm for marginal inference by optimizing the tree-reweighted variational objective over the marginal polytope. That feasible region enforces stronger consistency than the local relaxation used by some tree-reweighted methods. The aim is to improve inference by optimizing over a tighter description of the distributions that are possible.

The algorithm uses Frank-Wolfe updates and repeatedly calls a maximum a posteriori, or MAP, solver to guide its movement through the feasible region. This modular design makes existing exact and approximate MAP solvers usable as components of variational inference. A central mathematical difficulty is that the objective's gradients become unbounded near the boundary; the authors nevertheless establish global convergence and bound suboptimality for the proposed algorithm.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world instances show improved results from tightening the relaxation over both the marginal polytope and the spanning tree polytope. The contribution combines a convergence analysis for a difficult objective with a practical route for reusing MAP-solving machinery. The empirical findings support the value of imposing stronger consistency during inference.
neurips-2015-barrier-frank-wolfe-for-mar.tldr: A Frank-Wolfe algorithm uses repeated MAP calls to optimize a tighter variational inference objective, with convergence guarantees and improved empirical results.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization can require a difficult optimization problem inside the main optimization process. According to this paper, most existing approaches select their next step through an auxiliary nonconvex global optimization. That extra problem can be time-consuming and difficult to implement, making the machinery used to guide optimization a substantial burden of its own.

The paper introduces a method that removes this auxiliary optimization requirement. It also avoids delta-cover sampling, a requirement of an existing Bayesian optimization method with exponential convergence. The abstract describes that sampling requirement as having been considered impractical, so eliminating it addresses a second obstacle to using an approach with this convergence behavior.

The main result is that the proposed method achieves exponential convergence while dispensing with both requirements. The significance is the combination: the convergence result is retained alongside a simpler set of required operations. This establishes a route to exponential convergence that does not depend on either of the two specific computational components identified as problematic.
neurips-2015-bayesian-optimization-with-.tldr: The proposed Bayesian optimization method achieves exponential convergence without auxiliary global optimization or delta-cover sampling.

paragraphs: Combinatorial bandit problems involve repeatedly choosing structured actions while learning from limited feedback. This paper studies two versions with different assumptions about rewards and observations. In the stochastic version, semi-bandit feedback reveals information about the selected components. In the adversarial version, bandit feedback supplies information about the chosen action as a whole.

For the stochastic setting, the authors derive a problem-specific lower bound on regret, the performance lost while learning. They examine how this unavoidable cost scales with the dimension of the decision space. They also introduce ESCB, which exploits the problem's structure, and analyze its regret over a finite time horizon. Its guarantees improve on existing algorithms, and the reported practical results show substantial improvements.

For the adversarial setting, the paper introduces CombEXP. Its regret scales like that of leading existing methods, while its computational complexity is lower for some combinatorial problems. These are distinct contributions: ESCB improves performance guarantees in the stochastic setting, whereas CombEXP offers a qualified computational improvement while preserving the established regret scaling.
neurips-2015-combinatorial-bandits-revis.tldr: ESCB improves stochastic combinatorial bandit guarantees, while CombEXP preserves adversarial regret scaling with lower computational cost for some problems.

paragraphs: Precipitation nowcasting asks how rainfall intensity will change across a local region over a short period. This paper represents the task as predicting a sequence of spatial observations from an earlier sequence. That formulation makes both the arrangement of rainfall across space and its evolution through time central to the learning problem.

The authors introduce a convolutional LSTM by replacing fully connected structures with convolutional structures in two places: the transition from input to internal state and the transition between successive states. The resulting recurrent model is designed to represent spatial relationships while carrying information through time. They use this component to construct a model that can be trained end to end for rainfall prediction.

In the reported experiments, ConvLSTM captures spatial and temporal correlations better and consistently outperforms both a fully connected LSTM and the operational ROVER forecasting algorithm. These findings support the architectural choice of incorporating convolution into both transitions. The contribution is a forecasting formulation and a matching recurrent architecture, with empirical evidence that their combination improves precipitation nowcasting.
neurips-2015-convolutional-lstm-network-.tldr: ConvLSTM uses convolutional input and recurrent transitions to model rainfall sequences and outperforms FC-LSTM and ROVER in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper views a broad class of generative models as systems that make a sequence of decisions. Under this perspective, producing data is a process with successive choices, rather than a single prediction. The authors use that connection to extend an existing model and then investigate it through data imputation, the task of filling in missing information.

They formulate imputation as a Markov decision process and build neural networks that represent policies for that process. Training uses a form of guided policy search. Predictions emerge through repeated feedback and refinement, so the model's decision-making procedure includes opportunities to revise its developing answer across multiple steps.

The experiments show that this approach learns effective imputation policies across multiple datasets and problems of varying difficulty. Imputation also provides a setting for examining the relationship between unconditional generation and generation conditioned on available information. The paper's contribution is therefore both a connecting viewpoint for generative models and a concrete learning approach that makes iterative refinement part of the prediction process.
neurips-2015-data-generation-as-sequenti.tldr: Treating imputation as sequential decision making lets neural policies generate predictions through feedback and repeated refinement.

paragraphs: Categorical and multinomial models describe discrete outcomes, but many such outcomes are related across time or position. The paper points to dependencies among neighboring DNA nucleotides, the popularity of children's names across years, and changing or correlated topics in documents. The usual Dirichlet-multinomial formulation does not naturally express these kinds of dependence.

The authors combine a logistic stick-breaking representation with Pólya-gamma augmentation. Together, these constructions reformulate the multinomial distribution using latent variables whose likelihoods have a jointly Gaussian form. The key change is in the mathematical representation of the model: discrete observations become compatible with inference machinery developed for Gaussian models.

This compatibility opens access to a broad collection of Bayesian inference techniques with minimal additional overhead. The contribution is a reusable modeling and inference construction for dependent discrete data. Its importance lies in connecting two kinds of statistical machinery: the categorical distributions needed to represent observations and the Gaussian methods available for expressing and analyzing structured latent relationships.
neurips-2015-dependent-multinomial-model.tldr: Logistic stick-breaking and Pólya-gamma augmentation make dependent multinomial models accessible to Gaussian Bayesian inference techniques.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering groups observations so that each group lies approximately within a low-dimensional linear subspace. Although motivated by motion segmentation in computer vision, the method also appears in statistical learning tasks involving sensitive human data. This paper addresses how to perform that grouping while providing privacy protection through the framework of differential privacy.

The authors present two algorithms with different stated guarantees. One has formal guarantees for both privacy and utility, supported through theory and experiments. The other preserves differential privacy asymptotically and performs well in practice. The distinction matters because an asymptotic privacy statement describes limiting behavior, while the first method offers the stated formal combination of privacy and usefulness.

The analysis also yields new guarantees for agnostic subspace clustering and graph connectivity. These results arise during the privacy proofs but may be useful independently. Overall, the work connects privacy protection to a clustering task that seeks geometric structure, while examining whether the resulting groupings retain useful information and distinguishing the kinds of guarantees available for each method.
neurips-2015-differentially-private-subs.tldr: Two subspace clustering algorithms combine useful clustering with privacy guarantees, including one whose differential privacy guarantee is asymptotic.

paragraphs: In streaming active learning, a learner encounters examples over time and decides when to request labels. This paper develops an algorithm intended to make those requests more selectively while retaining broad theoretical applicability. Its guarantees cover arbitrary classifier representations and classification problems, including problems with severe noise.

The algorithm is built around a newly defined optimization problem. It can be implemented efficiently using an empirical risk minimization oracle, which supplies a classifier minimizing training error for the relevant learning problem. The efficiency claim is therefore tied to access to that oracle. The authors show that their approach is more aggressive than previous methods that satisfy both the same broad applicability requirement and this implementation requirement.

The paper also reports what it describes as the first experimental comparison of all efficient agnostic active learning algorithms. That comparison examines strengths and weaknesses across different settings. The contribution joins a more selective label-requesting strategy with an analysis of its guarantees and an empirical examination of how available efficient methods behave under different learning conditions.
neurips-2015-efficient-and-parsimonious-.tldr: A streaming active learner requests labels more aggressively while retaining broad noise-tolerant guarantees and efficient implementation with an ERM oracle.

paragraphs: Source separation seeks to distinguish underlying sources within combined observations. This paper introduces the infinite factorial dynamical model, a Bayesian nonparametric approach that can represent a potentially unbounded number of sources. Each source is modeled as a hidden Markov chain, and the chains evolve independently according to their respective dynamics.

The construction builds on the Markov Indian buffet process and accommodates either discrete or continuous source states. This flexibility lets the framework cover different kinds of evolving hidden processes. For posterior inference, the authors develop an algorithm using particle Gibbs with ancestor sampling, designed to apply efficiently across a wide range of source separation problems.

The method is evaluated on multitarget tracking, the cocktail party problem, power disaggregation, and multiuser detection. In these experiments, it outperforms previous approaches and handles problems that were computationally intractable for existing methods. The findings support both its modeling breadth and its computational usefulness in the evaluated applications, while the independence of the evolving source chains remains a stated feature of the model.
neurips-2015-infinite-factorial-dynamica.tldr: A Bayesian model with potentially unbounded independent source chains improves source separation across four evaluated applications.

paragraphs: Large-scale kernel methods can use Nyström subsampling to reduce the amount of computation required. This paper investigates what that reduction means for learning performance. Its analysis treats the data as randomly sampled and develops guarantees that hold with high probability, connecting the computational approximation to statistical learning behavior.

The main theoretical result is that Nyström approaches can attain optimal learning bounds when the subsampling level is chosen appropriately. That condition is central: the result depends on a suitable amount of subsampling. The analysis also suggests that the size of the approximation can serve as a regularization control, influencing how the method learns as well as how much work it performs.

The authors use this insight to motivate a simple incremental version of Nyström kernel ridge regression. In this approach, the subsampling level jointly controls computation and regularization. Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art performance on large benchmark datasets. The broader contribution is to show that a computational approximation can also provide a statistically meaningful way to regulate learning.
neurips-2015-less-is-more-nystrom-comput.tldr: Suitably chosen Nyström subsampling can achieve optimal learning bounds while using approximation size to control both computation and regularization.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs missing matrix entries from the entries that are observed. Extra features can help, and earlier theory had established substantial reductions in required observations when those features were completely clean. This paper asks what remains possible when the additional information contains noise or provides only weak guidance.

The proposed model balances information from features with information from observed entries. That balance is intended to retain the benefit of useful features while remaining robust to feature noise. The authors analyze general feature sets and show that the required number of observations can still be lower than for matrix completion without features, provided the features are sufficiently informative.

The empirical study uses synthetic data together with relationship prediction and semi-supervised clustering applications. The authors report improvements over other methods for matrix completion with features, alongside their theoretical comparison. The central implication is conditional but useful: side information need not be perfectly clean to reduce data requirements. Its contribution depends on how informative it remains, and the model explicitly accommodates the competing evidence from features and observations.
neurips-2015-matrix-completion-with-nois.tldr: Balancing noisy features with observed entries can reduce matrix completion's sample requirements when the features remain sufficiently informative.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate quantities defined by one or more probability distributions under nonparametric assumptions. Its targets include entropy, divergence, and mutual information: numerical summaries of distributions or relationships between them. The goal is to construct estimators for those summaries with favorable statistical behavior.

The authors derive their estimators using the von Mises expansion and influence functions, tools associated with semiparametric statistics. Influence functions describe how a target quantity responds to changes in the underlying distribution. This gives the paper a shared mathematical framework for developing estimators across several information-theoretic quantities, rather than treating each target as an unrelated estimation problem.

The paper analyzes versions based on data splitting and on a leave-one-out technique. Both achieve fast convergence rates and other favorable theoretical properties. Empirical evaluation also shows advantages over existing estimators. Together, these results support the framework at two levels: its analysis explains how estimation improves with data, and its experiments demonstrate useful performance for the information-theoretic quantities considered.
neurips-2015-nonparametric-von-mises-est.tldr: A von Mises and influence-function framework yields nonparametric information estimators with fast convergence and empirical advantages over existing methods.

paragraphs: Boosting combines weaker learning procedures into a stronger one. This paper extends that theory for regression to online learning, where predictions and updates occur over time. It makes the distinction between weak and strong learners precise through the losses they handle and the classes of regression functions against which they compete.

A weak learner handles linear losses and competes with a base class of functions. The main algorithm converts such a learner into one that handles smooth convex losses and competes with the linear span of the base class. This expands the comparison class to linear combinations of the original functions, giving a formal meaning to stronger predictive capability in the online setting.

The authors also provide a simpler algorithm whose comparison class is the convex hull of the base class, corresponding to convex combinations of its functions. They prove this simpler algorithm optimal. The two results offer different scopes of strengthening: the main construction reaches the linear span, while the simpler construction comes with an optimality result for the convex-hull setting.
neurips-2015-online-gradient-boosting-a3.tldr: Online gradient boosting converts weak regression learners into stronger learners competing with linear or convex combinations of their base functions.

paragraphs: Density ridge estimation aims to recover structural features of a probability density as a set. This paper introduces coverage risk to measure the error in that recovery. The measure extends the role of mean integrated squared error to set estimation, giving researchers a criterion for judging how well an estimated ridge represents the underlying structure.

The authors propose two estimators of coverage risk and show how to use them to choose tuning parameters. The procedure selects parameter values by minimizing estimated risk, connecting a practical modeling choice to the error measure being studied. They also analyze the convergence rate of coverage risk and prove that the risk estimators are consistent.

The method is applied to three simulated datasets and to cosmology data. In all reported examples, it successfully recovers the underlying density structure. These findings complement the theoretical results: the paper supplies a definition of estimation error, methods for estimating that error, and evidence that using it to guide parameter selection works in the evaluated examples.
neurips-2015-optimal-ridge-detection-usi.tldr: Coverage risk provides an error criterion and consistent risk estimators for tuning density ridge detection.

paragraphs: Exact maximum a posteriori inference seeks the highest-probability assignment in a graphical model. Finding that assignment can require searching a difficult space of possibilities. This paper investigates how parallel search can accelerate the task while retaining exact inference and working under a restriction on available memory.

The authors introduce SPRBFAOO, a parallel shared-memory recursive best-first AND/OR search algorithm. It explores the search space in best-first order, prioritizing the possibilities favored by the search procedure. Its design combines that ordering with restricted memory use and parallel execution, bringing these requirements together in a single method for graphical-model inference.

Experiments show that SPRBFAOO often outperforms the leading sequential AND/OR search approaches used in the comparison. The reported speed-ups reach sevenfold with twelve threads, with particularly strong benefits on hard instances. These are empirical gains rather than a claim of uniform acceleration. The results indicate that parallelism can substantially improve exact search even when the algorithm must also manage a limited memory budget.
neurips-2015-parallel-recursive-best-fir.tldr: A memory-restricted parallel AND/OR search method often accelerates exact MAP inference, reaching sevenfold speed-ups with twelve threads.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation concerns estimating the returns associated with following a policy. This paper proposes the Ω-return as an alternative to the λ-return used in TD(λ) algorithms. Its central motivation is that returns calculated over different lengths can be correlated, so the relationship among those estimates is relevant when forming an evaluation target.

The Ω-return explicitly accounts for those correlations. This makes the dependence between different-length returns part of the construction itself. The paper also identifies a practical obstacle: computing the Ω-return exactly is difficult. To make the idea usable, the authors suggest an approximation, connecting the proposed return definition to a computational approach.

Empirical studies suggest that the Ω-return is superior to both the λ-return and the γ-return across a variety of problems. The evidence is presented as suggestive rather than as a universal superiority guarantee. The contribution is a correlation-aware alternative for policy evaluation, together with an approximation and experimental support for considering how different return estimates depend on one another.
neurips-2015-policy-evaluation-using-the.tldr: The Ω-return accounts for correlations among different-length returns, with empirical studies suggesting advantages over λ-return and γ-return alternatives.

paragraphs: This paper proposes portfolio optimization based on quantile statistics to address extreme asset returns and limited historical data. The intended setting includes large portfolios, where estimating a suitable allocation can be difficult relative to the amount of available history. Robustness is therefore considered together with the scale of the investment problem.

The authors prove that the estimated portfolio's risk converges to the oracle optimal risk at a parametric rate under weak dependence among asset returns. Their theory does not require higher-order moment assumptions, allowing heavy-tailed returns. It also accommodates serial dependence, so the analysis is not restricted to returns that are independent across time.

The convergence result permits portfolio size to grow exponentially with the historical sample size within the theoretical setting. This quantifies the method's ability to handle high-dimensional problems rather than merely asserting that it works for many assets. Experiments on synthetic and real stock data demonstrate empirical effectiveness. Together, the analysis and experiments support a quantile-based approach to robust portfolio estimation under the stated dependence conditions.
neurips-2015-robust-portfolio-optimizati.tldr: Quantile-based portfolio optimization supports heavy-tailed, weakly dependent returns and large portfolios with risk convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Neuroimaging research uses brain observations to study relationships between biology and behavior. The paper identifies a separation in existing methods: some discover previously unknown neural structure, while others test structure associated with mental tasks. Studying larger collections of tasks creates a need for representations that support those task-related questions.

The authors combine representation modeling and task classification within one statistical learning problem. Their model uses multinomial logistic regression with factored coefficients and couples it to an autoencoder. These components connect the representation of brain observations to the classification of psychological tasks, making the two objectives parts of a unified model.

On a reference dataset, the approach produces neural models that are both more accurate and more interpretable. It also generalizes better to other datasets. These findings support learning representations together with the task classifier in this setting. The contribution is a specific statistical coupling between structure discovery and prediction, with reported benefits for understanding task-related neural models as well as applying them beyond the reference data.
neurips-2015-semi-supervised-factored-lo.tldr: Coupling factored logistic regression with an autoencoder improves the accuracy, interpretability, and cross-dataset generalization of neuroimaging task models.

paragraphs: Linear programming is widely used, but problems with very many variables and constraints can remain expensive for standard solvers. This paper proposes AL-CD, which combines an augmented Lagrangian method with coordinate descent. The approach is particularly relevant when the constraint matrix and the desired solutions are sparse.

The authors establish an iteration bound of O((log(1/ε))²), with each iteration costing O(nnz(A)), where nnz(A) counts nonzero entries in the constraint matrix. An active-set strategy can further reduce practical work to nonzero entries in columns or rows associated with active primal or dual variables. The computational benefit therefore connects directly to the sparse structure of the optimization problem.

Experiments use large linear programs from ℓ1-regularized multiclass SVMs, sparse inverse covariance estimation, and nonnegative matrix factorization. At a precision of 10⁻³, the proposed approach reaches solutions orders of magnitude faster than the compared interior-point and simplex implementations. These results establish a practical alternative for the evaluated sparse problems, alongside a complexity analysis explaining how sparsity affects its cost.
neurips-2015-sparse-linear-programming-v.tldr: Combining augmented Lagrangian optimization with coordinate descent exploits sparsity to solve evaluated large linear programs substantially faster.

paragraphs: Statistical model criticism asks how a fitted model fails to represent its data. Conventional approaches often require a practitioner to choose a particular statistic for detecting a mismatch. This paper proposes an exploratory alternative based on maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD, two-sample tests, which search analytically over a large collection of possible statistics.

The procedure selects the statistic that most clearly exposes a discrepancy within that collection. This selected statistic is called the witness function. Its role extends beyond indicating that a mismatch exists: it can help identify where the model misrepresents the observations. Synthetic-data demonstrations show how the witness function provides this more localized diagnostic information.

The authors also examine real-data models including restricted Boltzmann machines, deep belief networks, and Gaussian process regression. These applications reveal ways that the fitted models fail to capture properties of their training data. The contribution is an automated way to choose an informative diagnostic statistic and use it to explore the nature of a model's errors.
neurips-2015-statistical-model-criticism.tldr: MMD tests automatically select a witness function that helps reveal where a statistical model misrepresents its data.

paragraphs: Greedy algorithms build a solution through a sequence of locally selected steps. This paper studies what happens when the inputs guiding those choices are stochastic and their parameters are initially unknown. The learner must acquire that information over time while continuing to construct solutions, creating a learning problem inside the greedy procedure.

The authors introduce greedy regret and ε-quasi greedy regret to compare online performance with an offline greedy algorithm. That benchmark is important: the comparison measures the cost of learning relative to greedy performance. They propose one algorithm for each metric, using multi-armed bandit or pure-exploration policies at successive levels of the greedy process and learning from semi-bandit feedback.

Both algorithms achieve problem-dependent regret of O(log T), where T is the time horizon, for a general class of combinatorial structures and reward functions admitting greedy solutions. The authors also show that the bounds are tight in time and other problem parameters. This establishes that, within the analyzed setting, the learning cost grows only logarithmically and the stated dependence cannot generally be improved.
neurips-2015-stochastic-online-greedy-le.tldr: Two online greedy algorithms learn unknown stochastic inputs with tight logarithmic regret relative to offline greedy performance.

paragraphs: Object proposal generation searches for bounding boxes that might contain objects in an image. This paper treats the choice of an entire collection of boxes as a monotone submodular maximization problem. That formulation makes the value of adding a box depend on the boxes already selected, providing a framework for choosing a diverse set.

The search space contains quadratically many boxes in the number of pixels, making even a full scan for one greedy addition impractical. The authors replace that scan with a branch-and-bound procedure. They also extend lazy greedy selection to the branch-and-bound tree, aiming to speed up the repeated searches required to build the collection.

The formulation includes sliding windows with non-maximal suppression and Efficient Subwindow Search as special cases, connecting established heuristics within a common framework. Using a new diversity measure, the method achieves reported state-of-the-art empirical performance on object proposal generation. Its contribution combines a set-level objective with a search procedure designed to make greedy selection feasible over a very large space of candidate boxes.
neurips-2015-submodboxes-near-optimal-se.tldr: SubmodBoxes combines submodular selection, branch-and-bound search, and lazy greedy updates to find diverse object proposals efficiently.

paragraphs: When an image classification problem has many similar classes, requiring one correct guess can obscure whether a model has identified a useful shortlist. Top-k evaluation allows k guesses and checks whether the correct class appears among them. This paper develops a multiclass support vector machine specifically aimed at that evaluation criterion.

The proposed training objective uses a tight convex upper bound on top-k error. This gives the learning algorithm an optimizable surrogate tied directly to the desired shortlist performance. The authors also introduce a fast optimization method built around efficient projection onto the top-k simplex, a computational operation they identify as useful in its own right.

Experiments on five datasets show consistent improvements in top-k accuracy over the compared baselines. The findings support aligning the training objective with a task that allows multiple candidate labels. The paper contributes both the loss formulation and the optimization machinery needed to use it, with empirical evidence that this alignment improves the evaluated classifiers' ability to include the correct class in their guesses.
neurips-2015-top-k-multiclass-svm-1ec76e.tldr: A multiclass SVM trained with a convex surrogate for top-k error consistently improves top-k accuracy across five evaluated datasets.
